questions.q: What does 'blameless' actually mean in a blameless postmortem?
options: Blameless means only senior engineers are allowed to participate in the postmortem
Blameless means the postmortem process is entirely optional
No one is ever allowed to acknowledge that a mistake happened
The investigation focuses on the systemic reasons a mistake was possible and reached production, rather than assigning individual fault -- it doesn't pretend no human error occurred
questions.explain: Blameless doesn't deny that an engineer's change caused the incident -- it redirects the investigation toward systemic, fixable causes instead of punishing the individual, which is what keeps people honestly reporting issues.

questions.q: Why does a postmortem culture that punishes the engineer who made a mistake end up WORSE for long-term reliability, according to the lesson?
options: Punishing mistakes always improves code quality immediately
It teaches people to hide mistakes and near-misses, which removes the organization's best early-warning signal for catching problems before they become serious incidents
Blame-focused cultures produce faster root-cause analysis
There is no real downside to a blame-focused postmortem culture
questions.explain: If reporting a mistake leads to punishment, people stop reporting -- including near-misses that would otherwise surface a systemic problem before it causes a real incident.

questions.q: In the 5 Whys example, what is the REAL root cause of Northbeam's incident, five steps down from 'a bad deploy'?
options: An engineer was simply careless when writing the deploy
There is no process that periodically re-samples test data to keep it representative of the growing production knowledge base
The vector database itself was fundamentally broken
The company does not have enough engineers on staff
questions.explain: Each 'why' pushed past the surface explanation until it reached a specific, fixable PROCESS gap -- the absence of a mechanism to keep test data in sync with the evolving knowledge base.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say stopping the investigation at 'a bad deploy' leads to a vague, unenforceable response like 'review code more carefully'?
options: 'Review code more carefully' is actually the best possible response to any incident
A surface-level explanation doesn't point to anything specific and fixable, whereas the real root cause (missing test-data resampling process) leads directly to a concrete, buildable fix
There is no difference between a surface explanation and a root cause
Surface-level explanations are always more accurate than deeper root causes
questions.explain: A vague surface explanation can only produce a vague, unenforceable intention; a specific root cause (found via the 5 Whys) points to a specific, implementable fix with a clear owner.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what is the REAL deliverable of a postmortem -- not just a well-written account of what happened?
options: A dramatic, engaging narrative of the incident for other teams to read
A postmortem's only real deliverable is documentation, with no further action needed
A list of who is to blame for the incident
Specific action items, each with an owner and a deadline, that actually close the gap that caused the incident
questions.explain: A postmortem without owned, dated action items produces an interesting story but changes nothing about whether the incident recurs -- the action items, not the narrative, are what actually prevent recurrence.
